videos.title: Acid and Base Models: Arrhenius to Brønsted-Lowry | Year 12 Chemistry
videos.description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/chemistry/year12/module6/lesson01

Ammonia turns litmus blue, but it has no hydroxide. Follow how the definition of an acid changed: Lavoisier's oxygen, Davy's hydrogen, Arrhenius's ions in water, and Brønsted-Lowry proton transfer. See why each model was replaced, where the hydroxide in ammonia solution really comes from, how an acid and a base react as gases, with no aqueous solution, and the limit even Brønsted-Lowry has. Two exam-style questions at the end.

videos.title: How Mutation Adds a New Allele to a Population | Year 12 Biology Module 6
videos.description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/biology/year12/module6/lesson01

Did penicillin make bacteria resistant, or was resistance already there? Starting from Alexander Fleming's 1945 warning, see how one changed base in one cell becomes a new allele in a population's gene pool. Learn how that allele is passed on in bacteria and animals, why mutation is random with respect to need, what replica plates show, and how antibiotics select. Compare mutation with meiosis, fertilisation and gene flow. Two exam-style questions include brief feedback.

videos.title: How Mutagens Damage DNA: UV, X-rays, Chemicals and Natural Mutagens | Year 12 Biology Module 6
videos.description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/biology/year12/module6/lesson02

Sunlight damages the DNA in your skin cells every sunny day, yet almost none of it becomes a mutation. See how UV joins neighbouring thymines into a dimer, X-rays and gamma rays break strands, chemicals mimic, change or squeeze between bases, and natural mutagens act in similar ways or by inserting DNA. Learn how damage can become a lasting mutation, then try two exam-style questions, including UV and yeast data.
